visuals.title: Quiz
visuals.text: Five questions. Answer along on the cards below the transcript, then hear Marco's answers.

quiz.pause_at: Pause here if you want to think it through

questions.q: Five peers trade at 6x, 8x, 9x, 11x and 20x EBITDA. What's the median?
questions.explain: The median is the middle value, 9x. The average, 10.8x, is pulled up by the 20x outlier.
questions.explain_at: That's why bankers prefer the median

questions.q: Using that median, your target has EBITDA of 50 and net debt of 100. What's its implied equity value?
questions.explain: 9 × 50 = 450 of enterprise value, minus 100 of net debt: 350.
questions.explain_at: Then the bridge back to equity value, from episode nine

questions.q: Does a comps valuation include a control premium?

options.text: Yes, it's in the share price
Yes, when used in a takeover

questions.explain: Comps come from share prices for small stakes. Precedent transactions include what buyers pay for control.
questions.explain_at: Third trap. No. Comps are based on share prices

questions.q: Ferrari trades at about 19x EBITDA, the vehicles industry median about 8x. How many times higher is Ferrari's multiple?

options.text: About one and a half times

questions.explain_at: So Ferrari trades at more than twice a typical car maker

questions.q: Why can mass-market car makers be the wrong peers for Ferrari?

options.text: Ferrari makes too few cars to compare
Car makers trade at higher multiples
Its margins look like luxury goods

questions.explain: Ferrari's margins, pricing power and order book look like a luxury house, so volume car makers' multiples would undervalue it.
questions.explain_at: If you pick peers by the industry label alone
